items.q: A DSP lets an advertiser buy impressions from many sources through one platform.
items.why: One interface can reach many exchanges and SSPs.

items.q: A DSP bids on every impression it sees.
items.why: It bids only when the impression fits the targeting, budget and goals.

items.q: A DSP can apply frequency caps across the impressions it buys.
items.why: It can limit how often one person or device sees the same ad.

items.q: Bid shading lowers a bid toward the likely winning price in first-price auctions.
items.why: It helps the buyer avoid paying much more than needed.

items.q: Advertisers always pay the second-highest bid in today’s auctions.
items.why: Many auctions are now first-price, where the winner pays their own bid.

items.q: A DSP can buy both display and connected TV inventory.
items.why: Many DSPs cover several channels, including CTV and audio.

items.q: Pacing controls how quickly a campaign spends its budget.
items.why: Good pacing spreads spend across the campaign instead of using it all at once.
